title: Lesson 53: Reliability: Retries, Timeouts, and Circuit Breakers for LLM Calls
description: Separating transient failures from permanent ones, then applying the defense each failure class needs: retries with backoff and jitter, bounded timeouts, and a circuit breaker that fails fast to a fallback when a provider is genuinely down.

questions.question: Which failure should not be retried because retrying it only delays a fix?
options: A rate-limited response that will clear
An unauthorized response from bad credentials
A gateway timeout from an overloaded upstream
questions.explanation: An unauthorized response is a permanent failure on your side, like a malformed request or a wrong endpoint. Retrying it wastes time and hides the real configuration bug; only transient server-side failures are worth retrying.

questions.question: Why add jitter on top of exponential backoff?
options: Jitter removes the delay so retries happen immediately
Clients that fail together would retry in a synchronized spike
Jitter converts a transient failure into a permanent failure instead
Jitter guarantees the server's retry hint is always respected
questions.explanation: Backoff alone makes every client that failed at the same instant wait the same amount and retry together, re-creating the overload. Jitter randomizes the waits so the retries spread out across the window.

questions.question: What does an open circuit breaker change about a request to a provider that is down?
options: The request is rejected fast instead of waiting on a timeout
The request is buffered until the provider recovers
The request is retried more aggressively until it finally succeeds
The request is routed to a faster model automatically
questions.explanation: When the breaker is open, requests fail immediately or skip to the fallback instead of each burning a full timeout. That fast rejection is what separates a clean failover from a cascading slowdown.
